newsitem.title: USA: Pan Am buying Carnival Air, adding $60 million in financing.
newsitem.headline: Pan Am buying Carnival Air, adding $60 million in financing.

text.p: Pan American World Airways, a new company with a venerable name, announced a major expansion Friday, saying it would acquire its larger regional rival, Carnival Air Lines.

Specific terms of the deal, which followed two years of discussion, were not disclosed. But the companies said that Carnival Air's principle owner, Micky Arison, would invest $30 million in Pan Am, ending up with about 42 percent of the company's outstanding stock.

Pan Am also has arranged for a private placement of up to $30 million in a new series of convertible preferred stock, for a $60 million cash infusion that Pan Am Chief Executive Martin Shugrue said would go to working capital and for expenses such as bringing Carnival's fleet into compliance with Pan Am's and possibly toward acquiring additional aircraft.
Pan Am began operations last September with just two airliners. With the addition of Carnival's 27 jets, the combined companies will have a fleet of 31 aircraft, and 2,075 employees.
"We don't anticipate any layoffs at all," Shugrue told a news conference. "Neither one of these companies has a 30-year airline bureaucracy to deal with."

Carnival Air, which is not part of Carnival Corp., or its Carnival Cruise Lines, was formed in 1988 and is owned by Air Holding Corp. Arison also is chairman and chief executive of the separate Carnival Corp.
Pan Am, though it has proclaimed itself the successor to the venerable airline, began as a new company when it began flying last September.
Shugrue said he expected the acquisition would lead eventually to a larger company than the two as currently combined, but offered few specifics on his growth plans.
"Carnival flies its airplanes fewer hours per day than Pan Am flies its airplanes ... We fully intend to fly those aircraft for more hours per day," he said.

Shugrue said Pan Am would like to increase its frequency between New York and Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, to more than once a day and add a Miami-Dominican Republic route. He also said it would like to increase its New York-Los Angeles route to more than one per day and add routes to Kennedy Airport in New York and to California from Midway Airport in Chicago.
Carnival now has operations in South Florida, the Northeast, California and the Caribbean. It had about $270 million in revenues last year.

The privately held company does not release financial results, but Arison said it had not been profitable since last May, when Valujet Flight 592 crashed near Miami, killing all 110 people on board and diminishing the confidence of air travelers in newer airlines.
"We had been profitable until the Valujet situation," he said. But he said Carnival had posted consistent profits until then and Shugrue added that Carnival was "recovering nicely."

Arison also said he expected the Pan Am brand name would attract more business travelers. "Carnival has the distinct disadvantage as being primarily a leisure company because of its brand name," he said.
Last July Pan Am agreed to buy Carnival Air for about $100 million but called off the deal after PanAm examined the carrier's books and sought to rework the terms.
Shugrue and Arision would not specify what had changed since that deal fell apart.

Pan Am currently has a fleet of four Airbus A300's -- with two more to be delivered in the next two months -- flying between New York and Los Angeles, New York and Miami, New York and San Juan, Peurto Rico, Miami and Chicago, and Miami and San Juan.
It plans to begin service between New York and Santo Domingo on April 6.

The original Pan Am, one of the world's first airlines, went out of business amid a myriad of problems related to competition, its limited route structure, industry deregulation and finally, the bombing of one of its airliners over Lockerbie, Scotland in 1988.
Shugrue, who once headed the now-defunct Eastern Airlines, acquired the rights to the Pan Am name after the company went out of existence and later founded the new Pan Am, which is based in Miami.
Pan Am's stock fell 37.5 cents to $10.50 in afternoon trading on the American Stock Exchange, where it was among the most-actively traded issues.
